items.text:
• Settings
  • Runtimes
  • Projects, hosts and worktrees
path: Share skills, instructions and servers with every agent

items.title: Sign a runtime in
items.text: A runtime is the coding agent the app runs for you, such as Claude Code. Each one signs in to its own account. When one is installed but not signed in, the app says Needs signing in beside it, and you can sign it in from there.

items.title: Before you start
items.text: • The runtime installed on this Mac. See Runtimes for what each one needs and how it signs in.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. On a project's page, click the runtime above the prompt (it names the current one, such as Claude). A runtime that is not signed in says Needs signing in under its name. A runtime that says which account it is signed in with shows that instead, such as Claude Max or Anthropic API key.
  2. Choose Sign in, sign out, providers….

A sheet opens with the runtime's name and where it stands: Signed in and ready (or, where the runtime says which account, Signed in with Claude Max, and ready), Installed, and needs signing in, or Not asked yet. 3. If it needs signing in, click the way you want to sign in. The buttons are the runtime's own, with its own advice under each. - Most runtimes then sign in by themselves, often by opening a page in your browser. Finish there. Codex offers ChatGPT first: your browser opens OpenAI's sign-in, and once you finish, Codex in Terminal is signed in too. ChatGPT (device code) shows a code to enter on OpenAI's page instead, and API Key uses an OpenAI API key. Antigravity offers a personal or a business Google account, and opens Google's sign-in in your browser. - Claude Code signs in in Terminal: run claude, type /login, and follow what it asks. Then open the sheet again; it says which account, such as Claude Max. - Some hand you a command to run instead, and the sheet says, for example, Copilot signs in from a terminal. Run this: with the command under it. Click Open Terminal (it also copies the command), paste it and follow what it asks. Copy only copies it. When it is done, click I have done it. 4. The sheet should now say Signed in and ready. Click Done.

The runtime is ready for the next agent you start. An agent that stopped because it was not signed in can be prompted again.

When a runtime turns you away

You do not have to go looking for the sheet. When a runtime on this Mac refuses to start an agent or take a prompt because it needs signing in, the sheet opens by itself instead of an error. The same happens when nobody was waiting on it: a turn that is refused, a prompt that was queued, or an agent picked up again after the app restarts. The conversation says, for example, Claude needs signing in: it is not signed in, and the agent's turn ends with Its sign-in was refused. The agent keeps its conversation, so prompt it again once you have signed in.

If you close the sheet without signing in, it does not open by itself again for that runtime until a turn on it works. Open it from the runtime menu when you are ready.

Gemini: paste a key

Gemini signs in with a Gemini API key, not from the sheet: Google's own sign-in no longer works for individuals in Gemini CLI.

  1. Get a key at aistudio.google.com/apikey. It starts AIza or AQ..
  2. In Settings ▸ Agent Runtimes, paste it into the field under Gemini and click Save. The app checks it with Google and says Works or Refused.

It is kept in this Mac's Keychain and handed to Gemini agents on this Mac and on servers. A GEMINI_API_KEY already in your shell profile is used when Settings has none. Starting a Gemini agent with neither says Gemini needs an API key. Add one in Settings ▸ Agent Runtimes.

OpenCode: one provider at a time

OpenCode works signed out, on OpenCode Zen's free models, so its sheet says Signed in and ready from the start and still offers Login with opencode. Each sign-in adds one provider, such as Anthropic, OpenAI or GitHub Copilot, whose models then join the model menu.

  1. Click Login with opencode. The sheet hands you opencode auth login with the full path of the app's own copy, never a bare opencode, which could be another program of that name.
  2. Click Open Terminal, paste it, choose a provider and follow what it asks.
  3. Click I have done it. The provider's models are in the menu for the next agent.

To take a provider away, run the opencode auth logout command the sheet names in a terminal: OpenCode has no sign-out the app can call. A model you picked whose provider is not signed in is dropped when the agent next starts, and the conversation says so.

Choose who answers

Some runtimes can use more than one model provider. For those, the sheet has Who answers, listing them with a ✓ by the current one. Click another to switch. Turn off, beside a provider the runtime does not need, stops it being offered.

Sign out

  1. Open the same sheet and click Sign out. It is there only when the runtime is signed in and supports signing out from the app.
  2. Confirm with Sign out. The dialog says first whether anything is running on it, for example This stops 2 agents mid-conversation.

iPhone and iPad cannot sign runtimes in: sign in on the Mac. Signing Claude or Codex in on this Mac also signs them in on your Linux servers: their requests go through this Mac. OpenCode on a server borrows the providers this Mac signed in to with a key; a browser sign-in such as ChatGPT stays on this Mac, and the sheet says which. For any other runtime on a server, sign in on the server itself; see Add a server.

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• The sheet still says it needs signing in after I have done it. Close it and open it again; the app asks the runtime afresh each time. If it still says so, run the runtime's own sign-in in Terminal (for Claude Code, claude, then /login), then check again.
  • The runtime is not in the menu at all. It is not installed, or not where the app looks. With no runtime at all, the project list says No agent runtime found and what each one needs.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Runtimes
  • Keep going when a runtime runs out
  • Add a server

items.title: Sign in to an MCP server
items.text: Some remote MCP servers want you to sign in before they answer: GitHub's (https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/) is one. The app signs in as an OAuth client, the way the MCP authorization spec describes, in your own browser. The next agent you start has the server, with your sign-in.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: See which servers want it
items.text:
Open Settings ▸ Agent Configuration ▸ MCP servers, or Project Settings ▸ Agent Configuration ▸ MCP servers. A remote server that asked for a sign-in says needs sign-in on its row, the way a missing secret says NAME not set. Agents start without it until you sign in.

The app asks each remote server once, the first time the list is shown, with nothing sent but the MCP greeting. A server you have not approved yet in a project is not asked. A server whose entry sends its own Authorization header is not signed in to: the header is its sign-in.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: Sign in
items.text:
1. Choose Sign in… on the row.
  2. Your browser opens on the server's sign-in page. Sign in there and allow the access it asks for.
  3. The browser comes back to the app, says Signed in, and you can close the tab. The row now says signed in.

The sheet waits for up to ten minutes. Cancel stops it; nothing is kept.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: A server that doesn't let apps register
items.text:
Most servers let the app register itself for the sign-in. GitHub's does not: the sheet asks for a Client ID instead, and a Client secret if the client has one.

  1. Register an OAuth app with the server's sign-in. On GitHub: Settings ▸ Developer settings ▸ OAuth Apps ▸ New OAuth App.
  2. Give it the callback URL the sheet shows, http://127.0.0.1/callback. The app listens on a different port each time; GitHub takes any port on 127.0.0.1.
  3. Paste its client ID, and its secret, into the sheet, and choose Sign in.

The client is kept for that server's sign-in, so the next sign-in doesn't ask again.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: Add a server that asks, by hand
items.text: On Add by hand, Verify finds out the server wants a sign-in and opens the same sheet. Once you have signed in, it verifies again, with your sign-in, and Add is offered as usual. The entry that is written has no token in it.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: Sign out
items.text: Choose Sign out on the row. The app tells the server to forget the grant where the server offers that, and forgets it itself. The row says needs sign-in again.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: Where the sign-in is kept
items.text:
In ~/.agents-secrets/mcp-sign-ins.json, beside secrets.env, and like it readable only by you. The folder is apart from ~/.agents because ~/.agents is settings that you can copy, sync or commit, and secrets are not settings. Never in mcp.json, so a project's committed entry carries no one's sign-in. The app logs the server's name and what happened, never an address, a code or a token, and it never sends a sign-in to your iPhone, iPad or the web page. Do not copy, sync or commit ~/.agents-secrets.

A sign-in is for the server's address, so a server in both your own mcp.json and a project's is signed in to once.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: When an agent starts
items.text:
The app gives the agent the server with your sign-in as its Authorization header. A sign-in that is about to end is renewed first. If the server no longer takes it, the row says needs sign-in again, and agents start without the server until you sign in.

Signing in runs on this Mac's own host. A project on a server host can't sign in to an MCP server yet.
path: Sign in to an MCP server

items.title: Start a workflow from an MCP event
items.text:
An MCP server can offer events as well as tools and views: "a pull request's checks failed", "a message arrived". A workflow can run on one of them. This guide uses this project's own CI watcher, a small MCP server that turns GitHub Actions failures into checks.failed events, and the Fix failed checks workflow that starts an agent on each one.

The app asks servers for events in poll mode, following the MCP events draft (experimental-ext-triggers-events). A server that offers events only by push or webhook is shown as not supported yet.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A project with an MCP server that offers events. The CI watcher ships with Agents Host and the Linux host, and needs a signed-in gh (gh auth status) on the host. See Packages/MCPServers/README.md in the repo.
  • For every setting, see Workflow triggers and actions, and for what the event carries, Events from MCP servers.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Start the server
items.text:
Server events come from servers the project can already use: the project's .agents/mcp.json, your own ~/.agents/mcp.json, or a plugin. The CI watcher is in this project's .agents/mcp.json as ci, a local server the app hosts:

{ "mcpServers": { "ci": { "command": "ci-watcher", "hosted": true } } }
  1. In Project Settings ▸ Agent Configuration ▸ MCP servers, ci arrived with the project, so it is waiting for your OK: choose Approve. Until you do, it is asked for nothing, and the workflow's page says it is waiting for approval. See Add an MCP server from the registry.
  2. There is nothing to start. The app runs one copy of it on the host, the first time a workflow or an agent asks it something, and every agent shares that copy. It holds no token of its own: every GitHub call goes through your gh. See Share one copy of a local MCP server.

A local server without "hosted": true works too: the app runs its own copy of it to ask for events, with the same environment and secrets an agent gets, and each agent runs another for its tools.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Write the workflow
items.text:
A server's event is named the way the app's own are, noun.verbed, with no prefix. Under the name, the keys are the event's own filters, sent to the server:

---
name: Fix failed checks
on:
  - checks.failed:
      repo: alexec/Agents
agent: new
cooldown: 5m
labels: [ci]
---

A pull request's checks failed. The event's data says which PR, branch and jobs.
Use the `ci` server's `failed_log` to read each failed job. If it is a test known to be
flaky under load, use `rerun_failed`. Otherwise fix it on the PR's branch in a worktree,
push, and use `comment_on_pr` to say what you changed.
  • Without server:, the trigger listens to every server here that offers checks.failed. Add server: ci to listen to that one only, or server: [github, gitlab] for a list.
  • The ci server's checks.failed, pr.merged, pr.closed (closed without merging) and pr.conflicted (began to conflict with its base, #712) all take repo, branch (only that PR branch) and pr (only that pull request, by number). Left out, repo is the one the project's folder pushes to (#702). Given together, each must hold: {pr: 551} hears only PR 551's failures and merge.
  • Its pr.opened (#833) is raised when a pull request opens, or when a draft is marked ready for review. It takes the same filters and anyone. Drafts never raise it. The Review pull requests workflow in .agents/workflows/ starts an agent on it that reads the diff and leaves one comment.
  • checks.failed, pr.opened and the issue events are raised only for the repo's owner, members and collaborators, never a bot (#728). anyone: true raises them for everyone.
  • Its issue events, issue.opened, issue.labelled, issue.commented and issue.closed, take repo (optional, as above) and label; all but issue.opened also take issue, by number. On issue.labelled, label is the label added: {repo: alexec/Agents, label: bug} hears each issue as it is marked a bug.
  • A filter the server's event doesn't take, or a value of the wrong type, shows on the workflow's page as an error, naming the filters it does take.
  • This project's copy of the workflow arrives with enabled: false. Turn it on with its Enabled switch, and approve it.

Each event starts the workflow once, after its prompt. The agent is told the event's details and, in a fenced block, the server's data, marked as coming from the server and not from you. The workflow's prompt and permission mode decide what the agent may do with it.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Check it is listening
items.text:
Open the workflow's page, on the Mac, the iPhone or iPad, or the web page. Under Triggers, a line for each server the trigger listens to says how it is doing:

  • ci · checks.failed: Checked 20 s ago · last event 25 min ago: it is listening. A new subscription starts from now, so events from before it are not run.
  • Can't reach ci since 12:01 · trying again in 40 s, in orange: the server is down. The app tries again, waiting longer each time up to 5 minutes, and the line comes back by itself once the server answers.
  • A line in red says why it stopped: the server no longer offers the event, refused it, or doesn't take its filters. It is asked again once the file or the server's events change.
  • Events may have been missed since 09:14: the app was away longer than the server keeps events. Events it did get still run. Clear takes the line away.

Each event is also on the Events page, under the name checks.failed, with the run it started.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Turn it off
items.text: Turn the workflow off with its Enabled switch, and the app stops asking the server for its events. The CI watcher itself stops once nothing uses it: no agent's session has it open and no workflow listens for its events.
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Events
  • Workflow triggers and actions
  • Set up a workflow
  • Pin a page to a project: the CI watcher's board, ui://ci/board, can be pinned
path: Start a workflow from an MCP event

items.title: Start an agent in its own worktree
items.text: A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository, on its own branch. An agent in a worktree can edit, build and commit without getting in the way of you, or of another agent, in the project folder.
path: Start an agent in its own worktree

items.title: Before you start
items.text: • The project is a Git repository with at least one commit. In a folder that is not a repository, such as the chat project, the choice below does not appear. See Add a project and Chat without a project.
path: Start an agent in its own worktree

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Open the project's page.

On iPhone or iPad, tap the project to unfold it, then tap New session, the first row under it. 2. Before you send the first prompt, open the Worktree choice. On the Mac it sits above the prompt, beside the folder, and says Project folder until you change it. On iPhone and iPad it is the Worktree row of the start form. 3. Choose where the agent works: - Project folder: the folder itself, alongside anything else working there. The line under it names the branch the folder is on. - New worktree: A new branch from the last commit here. The app makes the worktree in .agents/worktrees/ at the top of the repository, on a new branch under agents/, both named from the first few words of your prompt. - A worktree already listed: join one that exists. The line under each says its branch and how many agents are working in it. - New worktree on a branch: make a worktree on a branch you already have, local or from a remote, marked From the remote. On the Mac every worktree and every branch is listed, and the list scrolls when there are more than fit. 4. Type the prompt and send it.

The agent starts in the worktree.

Move an agent that is already working

An agent that started in the project folder can move into a worktree later, or back out.

  1. Open the agent. On the Mac, the choice above the prompt names where it works: the branch the project folder is on, or the worktree's name.
  2. Open it and choose New worktree, a worktree already listed, or Project folder.
  3. If the agent is between turns, it moves at once. The conversation says where to, and how many uncommitted changes stayed behind.
  4. If it is working, the choice reads Moving to … and the move happens when its turn ends. Cancel move takes it back until then.
  5. Send the next prompt. The agent carries on in the new folder with the whole conversation, and the files, changes and row all follow it.

Agents can also move themselves, with move_worktree (see Tools the app gives agents). An agent that asks is moved when its turn ends and started again there to carry on, or left there asking to be archived if it also asked that.

Nothing uncommitted comes along: a new worktree starts from the last commit of the folder the agent is leaving, and what was not committed stays where it was.

An agent on Grok, Gemini or Antigravity cannot move: those runtimes can't carry their conversation into another folder, or haven't been checked. The choice is greyed out and its tooltip says why. Start a new agent in a worktree instead.

When the work is done

  1. Have the agent commit what it did, and merge or push the branch the way you usually would.
  2. Archive the agent. See Stop and archive agents.

If the app made the worktree, no other agent is working in it, and everything in it is committed, archiving removes the worktree. Its branch is deleted too if it has been merged; otherwise the branch is kept, with its commits. The conversation says which, for example Removed the worktree fix-login. Its branch agents/fix-login is kept, since everything in it was committed. 3. A worktree that still has uncommitted changes, or has other agents in it, is left where it is. It is listed under Worktrees on the project's page (on iPhone and iPad too). When you are done with it, archive the agents in it, then click Remove… beside it. If removing it would lose uncommitted changes or unmerged commits, the app says what would be lost and asks first.

Only worktrees the app made have Remove…. Ones you made yourself in Terminal are listed but left for you to remove.

On the project's page, Refresh worktrees updates the list after changes made outside the app. Clean up worktrees fills a new agent's prompt with a request to remove worktrees and branches for work already merged into the default branch. Review the request, then send it when you are ready.
path: Start an agent in its own worktree

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• New worktree is greyed out with There is no commit here yet to base a worktree on. Make a first commit in the project, then try again.
  • … is already checked out in … means that branch has a worktree already. Choose that worktree from the list instead of making a new one.
  • Remove… is greyed out: an agent is still working in the worktree. Archive it first.
  • The terminal says This shell is in … The agent now works in …: the agent moved while your shell went on in the old folder. The shell is yours and is never stopped for you; click Type cd there to follow the agent.
  • The session's row says Folder is missing, and sending to it says This agent's folder isn't there any more (…). It was a worktree, and may have been removed after merging. Its worktree was removed outside the app, for example by git worktree remove after a merge. What you typed stays in the prompt. Over the chat, and in the message, choose one of these:
  • Continue in the project folder starts a new session in the project folder on the same runtime, with the same name. The new session reads this one and carries on, with anything you had typed after that.
  • Recreate the worktree makes the worktree again from its branch, in the same place. It is offered only while the branch is still there. Send again afterwards.
  • Archive puts the session away.

The same happens to any agent whose folder has been moved or deleted, or is on a disk that isn't connected. Recreate the worktree is not offered for those.
path: Start an agent in its own worktree

items.title: Start workspaces from Agents
items.text:
Some servers stop: a cloud machine you turn off to save money, a Codespace that idles out, a Docker container you stopped. Usually a stopped server is just offline, and you have to start it yourself in the provider's console or in Terminal.

Give the control plane a workspace provider and link the server to its workspace. A stopped server then shows Start on every screen. The control plane starts the machine, waits for its agentsd to connect, and the server comes online by itself.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A control plane on one machine. The one on your Mac works. Several copies sharing a bucket can't run providers yet.
  • A server already added, or a workspace you can reach over ssh. See Add a server.
  • The provider's command-line tool on the Mac that runs the control plane, signed in: docker, doctl, gh, coder or gcloud. The provider runs there, not on the server. That is how it can start a server that is down.

items.title: Add a provider
items.text:
1. Open Settings ▸ Control plane ▸ Providers on the Mac and choose Add Provider….
  2. Pick the kind:
  3. Docker Containers: containers on the Mac that runs the control plane.
  4. DigitalOcean Droplets: droplets with a tag. Agents reaches each one as root@ its address unless you say another user.
  5. GitHub Codespaces, Coder Workspaces, or Google Cloud Workstations.
  6. Your commands: one workspace, given as the commands you already use to start and stop it, such as cws start devstack-1. A status command is optional; it prints running or stopped.
  7. MCP server: a provider of its own, or another MCP server with a tool map. See Add a workspace provider.
  8. Fill in its few fields. If it needs a token, add it under Secrets. A secret stays on the control plane and is never shown again.
  9. Choose Add. Agents checks the provider and lists its workspaces. If it can't, the sheet says why, in the provider's words.

items.title: Link a server to its workspace
items.text:
• For a server you already have: in Settings ▸ Control plane ▸ Hosts, open its ··· menu, choose Link to Workspace…, pick the workspace and choose Link.
  • For a workspace that isn't a server yet: start it, then choose Add as Host… beside it on the Providers page. Add a Server opens over ssh, with the provider's address filled in. The new server is linked to the workspace once it joins.

A workspace belongs to one server at a time: linking it to another moves the link.

items.title: Start a stopped server
items.text:
When a linked server's workspace is stopped, its row says Stopped and the strip over its chats says devbox is stopped, with Start. Press it on the Mac, the iPhone, the iPad or the browser.

The strip then says:

  1. Starting devbox… while the provider starts the machine.
  2. Waiting for devbox to connect… once it is up. If the server reaches the control plane through an ssh tunnel, the tunnel opens straight away.
  3. devbox started but agentsd didn't connect; starting it over ssh… if agentsd hasn't connected after two minutes. Agents starts it over ssh, as an install leaves it, and installs nothing.

The strip goes away when the server is online. A timer beside the words shows how long the start has taken so far. Pressing Start again on any screen while it starts does nothing more.

If the start fails, or the server hasn't connected after ten minutes, the strip and the row say why and offer Start again.

items.title: Stop a server
items.text: Choose Stop on its row in Settings ▸ Control plane ▸ Hosts. If agents are working there, Agents names them and asks first. The row says Stopping… and then Stopped.

items.title: Start when used and stop when idle
items.text:
A linked server's ··· menu has three settings:

  • Start when used, on by default.
  • Stop when idle, after 30 minutes by default.
  • Start for scheduled workflows, on by default.

All three are kept with the link.

items.title: Start when used
items.text:
With Start when used on, you don't have to press Start. Send a prompt to an agent on the stopped server, or start a new agent in one of its projects, on the Mac, the iPhone or the web page:

  • The control plane keeps what you sent and starts the workspace.
  • The chat shows your prompt as a dashed bubble, with Waiting for devbox to start under it. A new agent's chat opens at once with its first prompt waiting the same way.
  • When the server connects, the prompt goes, once, in the order it was sent. A new agent is made then, and its chat opens.

What was sent is kept by the control plane, not by the app. You can close the app or lock the phone, and it still goes. Up to 20 can wait for one server.

  • To take one back, press × beside it. The workspace keeps starting.
  • If the start fails, each waiting prompt says Not sent and why, with Try Again.
  • Attachments can't wait. Send the words alone, or start the server first.

Only prompts and new agents start a workspace. Reading a chat or a file on a stopped server doesn't. With Start when used off, a prompt to a stopped server is refused, and its strip offers Start.

items.title: Stop when idle
items.text:
A workspace costs money while it runs. With Stop when idle on, Agents stops it once its server has been idle for the whole time you chose: 15, 30 or 60 minutes, or 2 hours. Idle means:

  • no turn running,
  • no agent waiting on your answer,
  • and no terminal or project shell open.

A turn starting in that time starts the count again. When Agents stops it, its row and the strip over its chats say devbox was stopped by Agents after 30 minutes idle. With Start when used on as well, your next prompt starts it again.

A server on a build of Agents from before this never says whether it is idle, so it is never stopped as idle. Update it from its row.

items.title: Start for scheduled workflows
items.text:
A stopped server runs nothing, so its scheduled workflows would not run. With Start for scheduled workflows on, Agents starts the workspace a little before the server's next scheduled workflow is due:

  • The server's own clock still fires the workflow. Agents only starts the machine.
  • It starts it 5 minutes before the due time. After the first start, it uses how long the last start took, plus 2 minutes.
  • It starts it once for each due time.
  • Stop when idle does not stop a server whose next scheduled workflow is due within its idle time. After the run, the server is idle again and stops as usual.

A stopped server's row, and the strip over its chats on the Mac, the iPhone and the web page, say when it starts and for which workflow: Starts at 02:55 for Nightly review. Stop says it too, before it stops the server.

With the switch off, the server stays stopped, and its scheduled workflows don't run while it is stopped. Its row warns you of that when it has some and Stop when idle is on. A server on a build of Agents from before this doesn't say when its workflows are due, so it is not started for them, and its row warns you the same way.

Only scheduled workflows start a server. An event (such as issue.opened) is still heard only when the server is next up. Agents knows only the due time the server last sent: a workflow added while it is stopped is not seen until it is next up.

items.title: Make a new workspace
items.text:
For a provider that can make workspaces, its card in Settings ▸ Control plane ▸ Providers has New Workspace….

  1. Give it a name, and make its choices: its size or region, say.
  2. Choose Make…. Agents says what it will make and, if the provider says, what it costs.
  3. Choose Make.

The new workspace shows Joining… until it has installed Agents and joined. Then it is linked to its host. A provider that can't install on first boot opens Add a Server with the new workspace filled in, as Add as Host… does.

To delete one, choose Delete Workspace… in its server's ··· menu on the Hosts page. Agents names what is lost first: the workspace, everything on its disk, and the server with its agents.

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• The provider can't list. Its card says why, and shows what it last listed. Check its command-line tool is installed and signed in on the Mac that runs the control plane, then choose List Again in its ··· menu.
  • "workspace-commands isn't installed beside the control plane". This build of Agents Host doesn't carry the command provider yet. Set AGENTS_WORKSPACE_COMMANDS to a build of it for the control plane, or wait for a build that has it.
  • The server starts but never connects. Make agentsd start when the machine boots: on Linux, loginctl enable-linger $USER keeps the user's services running with nobody logged in. Or give the workspace an ssh address, so Agents can start agentsd itself.

items.title: Related
items.text:
• Add a workspace provider: presets, your own commands, a tool map, or a provider of your own.
  • Workspace providers: the tools a provider offers.
  • The control plane: why providers run there.

items.title: Use a shell in an agent's folder
items.text: Each agent has shells of its own, in the folder it works in, in the Terminal pane beside the conversation. Use one to run the tests yourself, look at git diff, or start a server while the agent works. On the Mac you can have several, one to a tab.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: Before you start
items.text: • An agent. Its shells open in its folder or worktree, on the Mac or on the server it runs on.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Open the agent's conversation, and open the sidebar with the button at the top right of the window (View ▸ Show Inspector, Option-Command-I).
  2. Click Terminal at the top of the sidebar, or press Command-3.

The first shell, Shell 1, is already open in the agent's folder. 3. To open another, click + (New shell) at the end of the tabs. It opens in a new tab, Shell 2, and takes the keyboard. Click a tab to bring it forward. 4. To close one, click the × on its tab (Close this shell). The last tab has none.

Closing a tab is the only thing that ends a shell. Changing pane, opening another agent, closing the window or quitting the app leaves every shell running, and the tabs are back when you return.

If the agent has moved to a worktree since the shell opened, the pane says This shell is in the old folder, and Type cd there types the cd to the new one for you.

On iPhone and iPad

Open Terminal from the conversation. It shows the agent's first shell, Shell 1, and has no tabs.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: A shell in the project folder
items.text:
Press Control-` (View ▸ Project Terminal) to open a shell in the selected project's own folder, on the project's Mac or server, under whatever page is open. It needs no agent: it opens with none chosen, and choosing an agent in the project leaves it where it is, in the project folder, not the agent's worktree. Another project shows that project's shells.

Click + (New shell) for another, in a tab of its own, as in an agent's pane. Press Control-` again, or click the down arrow, to hide them; they keep running. Click a tab's × to end that shell; closing the last puts the panel away. Drag its top edge to make it taller.

On iPhone and iPad, choose Project Terminal from a project page's … menu, or press Control-` on an iPad keyboard. It has the same tabs as the Mac. Done puts it away; End Shell ends the shell in front.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: Keys in a shell
items.text:
While a shell has the keyboard on the Mac, five keys are the terminal's, as in Terminal:

  • Command-. interrupts what is running, as Control-C does.
  • Command-K clears the screen and what scrolled off it.
  • Command-F finds in the shell's text.
  • Command-T opens another shell, and Command-W closes this one.

Every other shortcut works as it does anywhere else in the window: Command-N, Control-`, Control-Command-S and the rest of Keyboard shortcuts. You don't have to click out of the shell first. To stop the agent or find a session instead, click out of the shell, or use the menu.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• The project shell says There is no such agent. The project is on a server with an older version of Agents. The server updates when nothing is mid-turn there.
  • The shell is no longer running. It exited, for example after exit. Click New shell to open another.
  • + is greyed out. On a server with an older version of Agents, which holds one shell per agent. The server updates when nothing is mid-turn there.
path: Use a shell in an agent's folder

items.title: Use Agents in a browser
items.text:
Agents Host serves Agents as a web page, for a browser on the same Mac. The page is another screen onto your agents, like the window and the phone. You can read and answer agents, start and steer them, open their files and run workflows from a browser tab, without the window open. Safari and Chrome are tested.

Only a browser on this Mac can reach the page. Using it from another computer waits on serving it at a public address (issue #61).

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• Agents Host on this Mac, running the control plane here. See Set up Agents on this Mac.
  • A paired window, or Agents Host itself, to get a code from.

items.title: Open the page and pair the browser
items.text:
1. In the window, choose View ▸ Open in Browser. The same button is first on Settings ▸ Control plane, beside Use Agents in Safari or Chrome on this Mac, and in Agents Host beside Serve Agents to browsers on this Mac and in its menu.

The page, http://localhost:8792, opens in your default browser. The first time, it pairs that browser in the same step: there is nothing to copy or paste.

The page lists the projects on every host. With none yet, it says No projects yet, with Add Project… and Clone Project from Git URL… beside it. Its footer names the browser, as Chrome on this Mac. The window lists it under Clients as Chrome on followed by this Mac's name.

If the page isn't being served, nothing opens, and it says why, as Not serving: port 8792 is in use by another app.

items.title: Pair a browser by hand
items.text:
For a browser that isn't the default one, open http://localhost:8792 in it. The page says Connect this browser to your agents.

  1. Get a code, from either place:
  2. In the window, open Settings ▸ Control plane, click Show beside Clients, then click Pair a Browser….
  3. In Agents Host, click Pair a Window or Phone… and choose A browser on this Mac.

Click Copy. Whoever pastes the code can then do everything the window can, so paste it only into this page. 2. Paste the code into the page and click Connect.

The browser keeps a key of its own, which can't be copied out of it. Next time you open the address, it connects with that key, and nothing needs pasting.

items.title: What you can do there
items.text:
A paired browser may do everything the window may (#111). The page itself shows what the iPhone and iPad do, on every host:

  • read a conversation as it happens, at Outcome, Steps or Details, and answer permission requests and questions;
  • send a prompt with files or pictures attached, use Send now on a queued prompt, and change the mode, model or runtime;
  • start a chat with New Chat at the top of the + menu, in the host's chat project (see Chat without a project);
  • add a project with + at the head of the projects column: Add Project… chooses a folder on the host by typing a path or clicking into folders, and Clone Project from Git URL… clones an HTTPS or SSH address into the host's home folder. With more than one host, the menu names each one;
  • start an agent in the project folder or in a new or existing worktree;
  • stop, archive and bring back a session, archive one that asks to be archived, mark it read or unread, and add or remove its labels;
  • see a project's workflows and run one now;
  • open the agent's files and its changes, and follow a live page as the agent writes it, and type on it.

The tab's title counts the sessions that need you, as (2) Agents.

Settings, signing runtimes in, pairing and hosts have no screens on the page yet, so do them in the window. A folder can't be dragged in from Finder, and Clone Project from Git URL… doesn't fill in a copied address, because the page doesn't read the clipboard. The page has no terminal and no dictation.

items.title: Install it as an app
items.text:
The page installs as an app of its own, with the Blob icon and its own window:

  • Chrome: click the install button at the end of the address bar, or choose Cast, Save, and Share ▸ Install Page as App… in the ⋮ menu.
  • Safari: choose File ▸ Add to Dock….

Safari's app keeps its own website data, so it isn't paired by the tab's key: pair it once by hand, as in Pair a browser by hand. Chrome's app shares the browser's key. The page is served only to this Mac for now, so it can't be added to a phone's home screen until it is served at a public address (#61).

items.title: Forget the browser
items.text:
• From the page itself: click Forget This Browser… in the footer, then Forget.
  • From the window: open Settings ▸ Control plane ▸ Clients, click Forget… beside the browser, then Forget.

Either way it is cut off at once, in every tab. The page says This browser was forgotten. Pair it again to carry on.

Clearing the site's data for localhost, or closing a private window, also loses the key. The control plane still lists the browser until you forget it there.

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• This code has expired. Ask for a new one. A code works for five minutes. Get a new one.
  • This code has been used. Ask for a new one. A code works once. An address with #code= in it, from the browser's history, is one of these: choose Open in Browser again instead.
  • That isn't an Agents code. It starts agents-control:2:c: Something else was pasted, or a code for a host. Copy the code again from Pair a Browser….
  • This code is for another control plane. The code came from a different set-up from the one serving this page.
  • That code is for a window or a phone. Get one from Pair a Browser…. A code from Pair a Device… or Pair a Mac… works only for those. Get one made for a browser. It works the other way too: a browser's code pasted into a phone or a window says That code is for a browser on this Mac.
  • Can't reach the control plane at localhost:8792. Trying again. Agents Host's control plane has stopped. The page shows what it last knew, and catches up by itself when the control plane is back, with no reload.
  • This browser isn't supported. The browser can't keep a key that can't be copied out of it. Use the current Safari or Chrome.
  • The page doesn't load at all. Check that Serve Agents to browsers on this Mac is on in Agents Host, and that the address is localhost, not this Mac's network name. A page that says only Connecting… has a key and is waiting for the control plane to answer.
  • Chrome's console reports a Content Security Policy violation for /.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json. Chrome DevTools asks for that file by itself while it is open, and the page's policy lets it talk only to its own WebSocket. The page answers it with a 404. It is harmless and doesn't stop the page.
  • Not serving: port 8792 is in use by another app. Agents Host says this under the switch, and Settings ▸ Control plane says it too, when something else had the port first. Whatever answers at that address isn't Agents: don't paste a code into it. Quit what holds the port (lsof -nP -iTCP:8792) and press Try Again.
  • That isn't allowed from this browser. The Mac's Agents may need updating. An older Agents Host still judges the browser by a grant. Update it.
  • That host can't do that yet. It may need updating. The host is older than the page.

  • The control plane.

items.title: Have an agent wait for something
items.text: An agent can wait for something to happen, such as a branch moving, another agent finishing, or the Mac waking. It ends its turn while it waits, which costs nothing, and it is started again when the thing happens. This guide has an agent wait for main to move and then carry on.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• An agent on any runtime. Every runtime gets the app's wait_for_event tool; see Runtimes.
  • The names of everything an agent can wait for are on Events.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Tell the agent, in words, what to wait for and what to do afterwards. For example:
Wait for PR 640 to merge, then pull main and run the tests.
If it has not merged by 6 pm, tell me.

You do not need to know the event's name. The agent finds it, here pr.merged from the ci server with pr: 640, and sets a time limit: yours if you gave one, otherwise its own. Every wait has one, from 1 minute to 24 hours, so none can last for ever; when it runs out the agent is started again and can wait again.

Only two of the app's own events can be narrowed: branch.moved by branch, and person.away and person.back by why (locked or idle). Either can name more than one value, meaning any of them, such as {"branch": ["agents/fix-640", "agents/fix-641"]}. branch.moved is only raised for a branch an agent works on, never the project's default branch (#702): this Mac's main moves only when someone pulls, so a merge on GitHub would never wake it, and a wait on it is refused. Anything else, such as agent.finished with {"labels": "deploy"}, is refused saying what the event takes, so the agent fixes it rather than waiting for something that never comes. To wait for particular agents to finish, the agent names them in agents instead.

An agent can also wait on an MCP server's event, such as pr.merged or pr.closed from a ci server. Then where is what the server is asked for, such as {"pr": 640} (the ci server fills in repo from the project's folder), and the wait subscribes to the server until it ends. A name no server here offers, or a filter the server doesn't take, is refused with what the server does take. See Events from MCP servers.

  1. If the runtime asks permission to use wait_for_event, allow it. Claude and Cursor may ask, and Copilot always does.

  2. Check that it is waiting. Above the prompt, the chat shows a capsule such as ◷ Waiting for pr.merged on ci (pr 640) · since 14:02 · until 18:00. On the project page, the agent is under Waiting with the same line under its report.

  3. Leave it. When the pull request merges, the agent is started again with a message saying what happened and when, and it carries on with the tests. If the time limit passes first, it is started again and told that the wait timed out.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Stop a wait
items.text:
• On the Mac: click ✕ on the capsule above the prompt, or on the agent's line under Waiting now on the Events page.
  • Anywhere, including the phone and iPad: send the agent a prompt. A line above the prompt says Sending will cancel the wait on … before you do. The agent is told its wait was cancelled by your message, and can wait again if it still needs to.

Stopping or archiving the agent also ends its wait.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Things to know
items.text:
• One wait at a time. An agent that starts a new wait replaces its earlier one.
  • Any one of several. An agent can wait for several events at once; the first to happen wakes it. It can also wait for a whole subject, such as agent.*.
  • Nothing is missed. If more matching events happen before the agent is running again, it is told how many, and can look them up.
  • Its own project and this Mac. An agent can wait for its project's events and the Mac's, not another project's.
  • Time limits run from 1 minute to 24 hours.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Have one agent wait for another
items.text:
Agents do not announce events of their own. To have one agent go on when another is done, tell it to wait for that agent:

Wait for the agent titled "Build" to finish, then deploy the docs.

It calls wait_for_event with agents, and is started again with how the other agent ended. A workflow can start when an agent finishes too, on agent.finished: see Workflow triggers and actions.
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Events, for every name and its details
  • Statuses and groups, for Waiting and blocks under Needs you
  • Set up a workflow, to start a new agent when something happens
path: Have an agent wait for something

items.title: Watch an agent's background work
items.text:
While it works, an agent can start a command that keeps running in the background, such as a dev server or a long test run, or hand part of the work to a subagent of its own. Each one is listed over the prompt while it runs, and you can read it, or stop a shell, without stopping the agent.

Only Claude and Codex report what they start, so only their work shows in this list. When another runtime starts a subagent of its own, the agent is running it and this list stays empty; you can still read the agent's own account of it in the conversation.

items.title: Before you start
items.text: • An agent on a runtime that tells the app about its background work: today Claude and Codex. The app goes by what the runtime says about itself, not by its name.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
See what is running (Mac)

  1. Open the agent's conversation. While anything runs in the background, a block over the prompt is headed In the background · 2 (or however many there are). The agent's row in the list says so too, for example 1 shell, 1 subagent in the background.
  2. Read a row. Each has the name the runtime gave it, what it is running or was asked to do, and how long it has been going (0:37). Hover over the name to see a shell's whole command.
  3. Click Output to open what a shell has printed so far, or Steps to see what a subagent is doing, step by step, in the Background pane of the sidebar.

The conversation also says when each one started and ended, for example Started “Run the test suite” in the background and Shell “Run the test suite” finished, with Steps or Output beside it.

Stop a shell

Click Stop on its row. The row says Stopping… until the runtime has stopped it, then Stopped · 0:02. Nothing else the agent is doing stops.

A subagent has no Stop: neither Claude nor Codex can stop one on its own. Its row says stops with the agent. To stop it, stop the agent (Command-.).

Look back at what ran

Open the Background pane in the sidebar (View ▸ Background, Command-6). It lists what the agent has had in the background lately, newest first, including what has ended, each saying how: Finished, Failed, Stopped or Ended with the turn, with how long it ran. Ended rows have no Stop, but Output and Steps still open. Until the agent starts something, the pane says Nothing in the background.

On iPhone and iPad

On iPhone, a line over the prompt says 2 in the background ›. Tap it for a sheet with each one and Stop on shells; the sheet closes by itself when the last one ends. On iPad, the block over the prompt is the same as the Mac's. Steps opens a subagent's steps in a sheet of their own.

items.title: Background work ends with the turn
items.text: A shell or subagent belongs to the turn that started it. When the runtime is let go at the end of the turn, anything still running is marked Ended with the turn, and the conversation says so once. Claude keeps its turn open until its subagents have finished, so it is usually a shell that is ended this way.

items.title: If it doesn't work
items.text:
• Nothing is listed, but the agent said it started something. Its runtime does not tell the app about background work. Use the Terminal pane to see what is running in the agent's folder.
  • … can't be stopped on its own. Stop the agent to stop it. The runtime refused the stop. The row goes back to running; stop the agent instead.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
Complete lists of what the app has, each entry described the same way. For looking something up, not for reading through.

  • Statuses and groups: every status an agent can show, the group it sits under, and what you can do from there.
  • Runtimes: the eight coding agents the app can start, and what each can do in the app.
  • Tools the app gives agents: every tool an agent gets from the app, and whether you are asked before it runs.
  • Settings, and the Runtimes and Resources pages: every control in Settings on the Mac, the Runtimes and Resources pages, and what iPhone and iPad need.
  • Workflow triggers and actions: the workflow file format, every trigger and setting, and when a workflow does not run.
  • Workspace providers: the tools a workspace provider offers, and how the control plane checks and calls them.
  • Personas: the persona file format, where personas live, and what picking one does.
  • Events: everything the app records, for waits, workflow triggers and the Events page.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: every shortcut and menu command on the Mac.
  • Feature matrix of coding-agent apps: which apps for running several coding agents have which features, Agents included.

items.title: Tools the app gives agents
items.text:
The app gives every agent it starts a set of tools of its own, alongside the runtime's tools, on every runtime (see Runtimes). This page lists them all, in the order an agent sees them. Every runtime takes them over a local http address the app serves on this computer only, with a key only that agent's session holds; the key stops working when the session ends. Copilot uses its own follow-up suggestions instead of the app's.

The last column says whether you are asked before the tool runs. Where it says the app answers, the runtime's permission question is answered by the app and you do not see it. Where it says the runtime decides, you get the same permission card as for any other tool if the runtime asks; Claude and Cursor ask, and Copilot asks before every tool call.

There's no tool for ending a turn. The app works out how each one ended: Complete, or Waiting on your answer when a question card is open or the agent's last words ask one, with the first sentence of its last message under its name (the question, when it waits on one). A turn that stopped short (cancelled, refused, out of tokens, failed) shows how it stopped instead. The conversation's name comes from the runtime, or from your first prompt when the runtime sends none. An agent that needs you asks, with its own question tool or ask_form. finish_turn was removed; a conversation that began before then can still call it, and what it says is kept.

Tool What it does Asks the person first? show_file Opens a file in the files pane beside the conversation, at a line. A Markdown file opens as a page that follows the agent's edits; an HTML file opens rendered, with scripts and the network off (see Look at an HTML page). The file must be inside the folders the agent was given. If you are reading another conversation, it waits until you open this one. No. The app answers. manage_workflows Lists, reads, writes and removes this project's workflows, and turns them off and on. A workflow an agent writes or changes appears on the project page straight away, waiting for your OK: it does not run until you click Approve, and you can archive it instead. A new one an agent writes also starts turned off, and its page says Off: written by an agent until you turn it on. An agent can turn any workflow off, but can turn back on only one an agent turned off: one you turned off, one an agent wrote, and one whose file says enabled: false for any other reason stay off until you turn them on. Off and archived are lines in the workflow's own file (enabled: false, archived: true), so turning one off writes that file; an agent's rewrite of a workflow keeps whatever those lines said. A project may have at most three workflows waiting for your OK; an agent writing a fourth is refused until you approve or remove one. Approved ones don't count. See Workflow triggers and actions and its limits. No. The app answers. ask_form Asks you a question or a short form and waits for your answer. Reaches you on the Mac or on your phone. Used when the runtime has no working ask tool of its own, or when that tool never reaches the model. No. The app answers. start_session Starts another session in this project with a prompt of its own, marked as started by this session. It can choose the runtime, model, a permission mode no looser than its own, and whether to work in the project folder, a new worktree, an existing worktree or a branch. If the project would go over either of its two helper limits, how many may be running and how many may exist not yet archived (3 and 5 unless you set them in Project Settings ▸ General), the session is queued instead, and the answer says which limit, names the sessions holding it and gives its place in the queue. A queued session runs nothing until a running place and a not-archived place are both free, behind working and waiting agents, and then starts by itself, oldest first; it shows under Waiting as Queued, 1st, Queued, 2nd and so on, and survives a restart. Past the third limit, how many may be queued (5 unless you set it), the start is refused, naming the limits and sessions. A runtime that can't take an agent on this Mac (not installed, not signed in, or out of the pool on the Agent Runtimes page) is refused before anything starts, with the reason and the runtimes that can; so is a model the runtime doesn't offer, naming the ones it does. With no runtime named, it starts on Claude, which is checked the same way. The runtime decides. stop_session Stops a session this agent started, or one below it, as your Stop would. That frees its running place; it keeps its not-archived place until it is archived. A queued one is taken off the queue and never starts; so is one you or the agent archives. The runtime decides. archive_session With no id, archives the agent's own session once its turn ends, if the turn ends Complete, Nothing to do or Partly done; an ending that asks you something else (a question, stuck, blocked) drops it, and so does anything you send first. Where it needs your approval, the session then carries an Archiving needs approval mark and is listed in Needs You, with a card at the end of its chat, until you click Approve (see Statuses and groups). A workflow's run its workflow lets archive itself (when-done: archive-allowed or archive, see When a run is done), or a session started by another in a project where sessions may archive the sessions they started, is archived without your approval, if the turn ends Complete or Nothing to do. It goes with move_worktree: the agent moves, and stays there waiting for approval instead of being started again. With an id, for a session this agent started or one below it, once its work is merged or abandoned: where Sessions may archive the sessions they started is on in Project Settings ▸ General (on unless you turn it off), it is archived now, as your Archive would, or when its turn ends if it is still working (if that turn ends Complete or Nothing to do; otherwise it waits for your approval). Its conversation says which agent archived it, agent.archived says by another agent, and you can bring it back from Archived. Where the switch is off, it waits for you to approve archiving it. Either way its running place is freed once its turn has ended; it keeps its not-archived place until it is archived. Refused, in words, for your own sessions, a workflow's, and sessions not below this agent. The runtime decides. move_worktree Moves the agent once its turn ends. On Claude, Copilot, Cursor and Codex only: the runtimes that can carry the conversation into another folder. worktree names a new worktree of the project or gives the path of one that exists, and leave_worktree (keep or remove) goes back to the project folder. Neither takes back a move it asked for. The agent is started again there to carry on, unless it also asked to be archived. A move doesn't go with a wait or with Waiting on your answer. Nothing uncommitted comes along. Removing takes the branch too when the app made it and it is merged; an unmerged branch is kept with its commits, so a lane can remove its worktree as soon as its work is committed. Removing is refused for a worktree the app did not make, another agent works in, or that is detached or whose branch is gone (its commits would be on no branch), and, unless the agent says to discard, when anything in it is uncommitted. The refusal names the files. The runtime decides. set_session_labels Adds or removes labels the agent owns on its own session, at once. It cannot remove or claim one of yours. The runtime decides. list_sessions Lists the sessions in this project, most recent first, its own included: each one's id, title, runtime, status, worktree and branch, the resources it holds, and what it last said. Nothing from another project. With started_by: me, it lists only the sessions this agent started, and the ones below them, that are not archived (one it did not start itself says who did), what each is doing and last said, after how many of the project's running and not-archived places are in use, such as "2 of 3 running, 4 of 5 not archived", with ", 2 of 5 queued" once any are. A queued one says queued (position 1). It ends with the runtimes start_session can start one on here, as of that moment, each with its model where this project has used it, and why each of the others can't. No. The app answers. read_session Reads one session in this project, by its id or exact title: what you asked, what the agent said, the tools it ran and the files they touched, what it said of how the work went, and its plan as it last stood. A long one keeps the first request and the latest turns and says how many were left out. Reading it changes nothing. A title used twice, a deleted session, or one not in this project is refused in words. Used when you ask an agent to continue another session's work. No. The app answers. message_session Sends words to another session in this project, by its id or exact title. It reads them as a prompt marked as the sender's, and its chat shows them as "From" that agent on the Mac, the Remote and the web. A session that is working reads it after its turn; one that is done is woken by it, yours included, within the project's running limit for sessions started by sessions; one that is stopped, or one waiting on your answer, is not woken: the message waits in its chat for you. It never answers a question or permission card. Limits: 4,000 characters, 30 messages an hour per sender, and at most 3 messages between agents in a row with no prompt from you; your next prompt starts the count again. Raises agent.messaged. No. The app answers. lease_resource Takes a turn with something only one agent should use at a time: a simulator, a browser, the screen, or anything it names. Waits up to 45 seconds if someone else holds it, then keeps the agent's place in line. A lease lasts 30 minutes unless the agent asks for up to 240 (or the declared resource's own lengths), and calling it again extends it. A declared resource may allow more than one holder at once. The runtime decides. release_resource Gives back a lease, or leaves the line for one. The runtime decides. list_resources Lists what can be leased on this Mac, and who holds or is waiting for what. Resources declared in Settings ▸ Resources come first, with their descriptions, even when free; the agent is told to lease one whenever its description applies. The runtime decides. wait_for_event Waits until something happens in this project or on this Mac, such as agent.finished, branch.moved, or mac.wake, optionally narrowed by a filter: branch on branch.moved or why on person.away and person.back (one value, or a list meaning any of them, such as {"branch": ["main", "develop"]}; checked against the event's inputSchema with the same checker as an MCP server's event's, so any other key, or a value a filter cannot have, is refused in the same words, naming what it takes) and with a time limit, until_minutes, of 1 minute to 24 hours, which every wait needs: one without it is refused, so no wait can last for ever. The call waits up to 45 s; after that the agent can end its turn, which costs nothing, and it is started again when the event happens or the time runs out. One wait per agent; a new one replaces the old. Also lists recent events, and with action list every event it can wait for in one list: the app's, then the project's MCP servers', each a line of JSON in events/list's shape (name, source, description, inputSchema, payloadSchema). A woken agent's details are named as the payloadSchema names them. Named agents instead of events, by id or exact title, it is a block: the agent's turn ends at once, it shows as Blocked, and it is started again, told how each one ended, once every one has finished, or the first with wake_on: any, when it is told which are still running. until_minutes is needed here too: with agents, or on its own, it starts it again then anyway, to check on something the app can't see, like a CI run, or a helper still running, which it can wait on again; message is what its row says meanwhile. See Events. The runtime decides. cancel_wait Stops the agent's wait, so nothing starts it again for it. The runtime decides. list_workspaces Lists the machines the control plane's hosts run on, from every workspace provider: each workspace's state, the host it is linked to and that host's state, and, for a provider that can make workspaces, the choices a new one takes. Never a provider's secrets. On a host that isn't on a control plane, it says there are none. See Start workspaces from Agents. The runtime decides. start_workspace Starts the workspace a host runs on, by the host's name. It answers at once; the host is up when it connects, which the agent can wait for with wait_for_event on server.online. The runtime decides. stop_workspace Stops the workspace a host runs on, and every agent there with it. While agents are working there it is refused, naming them, unless the agent says confirm_running. The runtime decides. make_workspace Makes a new workspace at a provider that can, with its choices; it joins as a host of the same name. It may cost money while it runs. Yes, always. A question card on every client, and nothing is made without your Make it. delete_workspace Deletes the workspace a host runs on, with everything on its disk, and removes the host with its agents. Yes, always. A question card on every client, and nothing is deleted without your Delete it.

set_session_labels adds or removes labels owned by the agent. start_session can give the new session up to five labels, which it owns from its first moment. Labels are unique within a session without regard to case. An agent cannot remove or claim a person-owned label; the whole call is refused if it tries. See Label a session.

start_session, stop_session, archive_session and list_sessions with started_by: me are given to every agent, including one another agent started (#940). The project's helper limits are the bound: they count every session an agent started, whoever started it. An agent can stop, archive and list the sessions it started and every session below them (the sessions those started, and so on), never your sessions, a workflow's, or another agent's. Each session keeps its direct starter, so the chain shows who started whom. Archiving or stopping an agent leaves the sessions it started working; every agent above it, and you, can still stop or archive them. Every agent is told, once at the start, to ask to archive its own session in its last turn, once its work is merged or abandoned and cleaned up (#703).

Before #638 these were start_agent, stop_agent, request_archive, archive_agent, list_my_agents and message_agent (and park_agent before request_archive). They are no longer offered or answered; a conversation that called them still shows those calls as the app's own.

A session started by another counts as running while it is working, waiting on a question or permission, starting, or waiting to carry on by itself: blocked on other agents or a time, waiting on events, or waiting for an allowance. Finished, stopped and archived helpers don't, nor does one waiting for archive approval. So a lead that stops a helper whose part is done, or archives it, frees a running place once its turn has ended; the helper's not-archived place stays taken until it is archived. A lead should archive a helper once its work is merged or abandoned, rather than remove the helper's worktree under it; archiving removes a worktree the app made for it once everything in it is committed. Both limits are yours alone to change: the tools only read them. They are kept in the project's .agents/project.json; a value written there by hand is held to the maximums. list_sessions, read_session and message_session are given to every agent, including one another agent started.

The five workspace tools are given to every agent. The control plane does what they ask as it would for you, and its log names the agent that asked. Agents reach providers only through the control plane, never directly.

items.title: The writer's tools
items.text:
The agent that writes a provider's map at Add Provider (#858) has these seven tools and no others, of the app's or of its runtime's. No other agent has them. The control plane answers each one, with every secret's value replaced by ${NAME}.

Tool What it does Asks you first? read_tools The MCP server's tools: names, descriptions, input schemas and annotations. No. read_help ‹cli› ‹words…› --help, for at most three subcommands that the help printed. No. check_draft Checks a map or config as Add does, with one list. Only when the list may change something: Run Check. prove_start, prove_stop Starts or stops one workspace from the last list with the draft. Yes, always, in the sheet. send_draft The result, with a note of up to three lines. No. give_up Ends with a reason. No.
